knitr::opts_chunk$set(

  comment = "#>"

In this article, you will learn how to write a function for a single instance and apply it to a whole batch with `vectorize()`.

## Mapping a Function over a Batch

Many computations are easiest to write for one instance: one observation, one parameter vector, one sequence.
`vectorize()` takes such a function and returns one that maps it over an axis of its arguments, much like `base::Vectorize()`.
Unlike `Vectorize()`, it does not call the function once per instance.
It traces the function once and turns every operation into one that works on the whole batch, so the result runs as a single program.

Below, `f` computes the squared norm of a single vector.
Vectorized, it computes one norm per row of a matrix:

```{r}
library(anvl)

f <- function(x) sum(x^2)
x <- nv_array(matrix(1:6, nrow = 3L), dtype = "f32")

jit(vectorize(f))(x)
```

As with `gradient()`, the result of `vectorize()` must be called inside `jit()`, because it transforms the traced program of `f`.

## Choosing the Batch Axes with `in_axes`

By default, `vectorize()` maps over axis `1` of every argument that is an array.
`in_axes` changes this.
A single axis applies to all of them, so `in_axes = 2L` maps over the columns instead:

```{r}
jit(vectorize(f, in_axes = 2L))(x)
```

A named list gives each argument its own batch axis.
An argument that the list leaves out or gives `NULL` is passed to every application of `f` unchanged.
Here, every row of `x` is multiplied by the same weights `w`:

```{r}
g <- function(x, w) sum(x * w)
w <- nv_array(c(2, -1), dtype = "f32")

jit(vectorize(g, in_axes = list(x = 1L)))(x, w)
```

All arguments that are mapped over must have the same size along their batch axes.
Every array in a nested argument uses that argument's batch axis.

## Placing the Batch Axis with `out_axes`

The outputs are stacked along axis `1` by default.
`out_axes` puts the batch axis elsewhere.
A single axis applies to every output, and a list that follows the structure of the output gives each part its own axis.
`NULL` returns an output as it is, which is allowed for an output that does not depend on the arguments mapped over:

```{r}
h <- function(x, w) list(scaled = x * w, total = sum(w))

h_vec <- vectorize(h, in_axes = list(x = 1L), out_axes = list(scaled = 2L, total = NULL))
jit(h_vec)(x, w)
```

## Composing with Other Transformations

`vectorize()` composes with `gradient()` and with itself.
A common use is computing one gradient per observation, e.g. to clip them individually.
The loss below is written for a single observation `x`; vectorizing its gradient over `x` gives the gradient of every observation with respect to the shared parameters `w`:

```{r}
loss <- function(w, x) sum(x * w)^2
per_example_grad <- jit(vectorize(gradient(loss, wrt = "w"), in_axes = list(x = 1L)))

per_example_grad(w, x)
```

Nesting two calls maps over two axes, here forming all pairwise products of two vectors:

```{r}
outer_product <- vectorize(vectorize(function(a, b) a * b, in_axes = list(b = 1L)), in_axes = list(a = 1L))
jit(outer_product)(nv_array(c(1, 2, 3), dtype = "f32"), nv_array(c(10, 20), dtype = "f32"))
```

## Control Flow

Control flow can depend on the arguments mapped over.
Each instance may then take a different path, which `vectorize()` resolves in the way you would by hand:
`nv_if()` evaluates each branch that some instance takes and selects the result of each instance, and `nv_while()` runs until the condition is `FALSE` for every instance, keeping the state of the instances that finished earlier.
A branch, or the loop body, then also runs for instances that do not take it, so side effects such as printing happen for them too; a branch runs such an instance on the inputs of one that does take it.
Their results are discarded, and gradients are those of each instance's own path.
Below, each instance halves its value until it is smaller than one, counting the steps:

```{r}
halvings <- function(x) {
  nv_while(
    list(x = x, n = nv_scalar(0L)),
    function(x, n) x >= 1,
    function(x, n) list(x = x / 2, n = n + 1L)
  )$n
}

jit(vectorize(halvings))(nv_array(c(0.5, 3, 20), dtype = "f32"))
```

## Limitations

`vectorize()` needs a rule for every primitive that a value mapped over goes through.
The decompositions `prim_qr()`, `prim_lu()`, `prim_svd()` and `prim_eigh()` have none yet, so they can only be applied to values that are not mapped over.
Nor can the start indices of `prim_dynamic_slice()` and `prim_dynamic_update_slice()`, or the padding value of `prim_pad()`, be mapped over yet.
A few primitives cannot work on the whole batch at once and are applied to one instance after the other in a loop instead: `prim_rng_bit_generator()` mapped over its state, `prim_reduce()` mapped over its initial value, and a grouped `prim_convolution()` mapped over its kernel.
See `?vectorize` for details, and `?rule_vectorize` for adding a rule to a primitive of your own.
